content: Lust refers to any intense desire or craving for gratification and excitement. While it is often associated with sexual desire, the term can also be used to describe a lust for men, lust for blood (commonly referred to as bloodlust), lust for power, or even a lust for love. The Greek word epithymia (ἐπιθυμία), which translates to lust, can also be interpreted as to covet in English. Lust in the Context of Religion Christianity — General In Catholic tradition, lust is considered one of the primary sins or vices. In the Old Testament, adultery was a crime punishable by stoning. In the New Testament, Jesus expanded the definition of adultery to include looking at a woman with lustful intent, as stated in Matthew 5:28. The woman in this context refers specifically to a married woman. Christianity — Protestantism Protestants believe that all sins, including lust, can only be forgiven by God through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. If an individual places their faith in Jesus as their sole Savior, they will receive His righteousness and gain entry into heaven, regardless of their past actions. However, to enter God's heaven, one must also receive the Spirit of God. This is illustrated in Luke 7:36-50, where Jesus forgives a sinful woman. Punishment in the Afterlife According to some Christian sources, individuals whose primary unforgiven sin is lust are punished in Hell by being smothered in fire and brimstone. While most Christian traditions agree that the damned will face punishment in Hell for their sins, the exact nature of this punishment is speculative. The principal torment is believed to stem from being completely separated from God. In Dante's Inferno, the first part of The Divine Comedy, the lustful are punished by being perpetually swept around in a whirlwind, symbolizing their uncontrollable passions. Repentance in Purgatory In The Divine Comedy, penitents guilty of lust cleanse their souls by walking through flames, which purges their minds of all lustful thoughts. Judaism In traditional Judaism, everything on Earth is believed to have been created with a purpose, including basic human drives. Lust is considered sinful only when it is directed toward another man's possessions or wife. However, lusting after one's own spouse is not only not sinful but is regarded as a mitzvah, a good deed or commandment. Symbolic Representations The sin of lust is often symbolized by the color blue, as seen on the cover of the book Lust in The Seven Deadly Sins series published by Oxford University Press. Another common symbol of lust is the cow or bull, as depicted in the 16th-century engraving Shamelessness by Georg Pencz. Additionally, lust is represented in the Thoth Tarot deck by Aleister Crowley, specifically in the card titled Lust, which is the eighth card in the Major Arcana.
